itsuki.title: Itsuki's Road — the Kuroda
acts: Open: the family silence, broken for you
Deepen: a Tower house that does not give second chances
Converge: asking him to use his sight on Gin

beats.scene: Geidai, an hour before the cleaners
prose: You call Itsuki because he is the one door in your life that has never had a lock you did not already hold the key to. It is not yet five, the kettle in your brother's kitchen is still cold behind you, and the line connects on the second ring the way it always has — not because he was awake, but because some part of him has spent fifteen years listening for the particular weight of you on the other end of a phone. Rei. Not a question. Already he is pulling a paint-stiff sleeve over his wrist, already moving through the dark of the studio toward the lamp, and you can hear in the rustle of him the decision being made before you have asked for anything: that whatever this is, he will carry his half of it.

The studio at Geidai holds the cold of a room nobody has slept in, linseed and the dregs of convenience-store coffee, canvases leaned three deep against every wall. Every third one is the same overpass at Ōji — painted, scraped back, painted over, each version wrong in a way he has never been able to name and never once agreed to sell. You tell him about the empty hook where Gin's coat should be, the briefing skipped, the address in no file, the voice on the twentieth call that was your brother's voice the way a photograph is a face. You do not soften any of it, because Itsuki has never once thanked you for softening a thing.

He listens the whole way through without interrupting, which is its own kind of answer, and when you finish there is a silence with a shape to it — the shape of a man counting the doors he is willing to open and the ones the opening will cost him. Then, quietly, in the voice he uses for true things: There are two ways a Kuroda puts you across a sleeping city, and neither of them is free. Tell me which kind of debt you can stand to owe by morning.

choices.x: "The family's way. True teleportation — Sei's reach."
choices.hint: The oldest house in Tokyo will fold the city around you in an instant. It will also decide, at its leisure, what the crossing cost — and the Kuroda do not forgive a debt, they file it.

choices.x: "Your way. Through a painting."
choices.hint: Itsuki's gift never opened clean; he reaches through the canvases instead, a forgery of the real thing. It is gentler to the family and ruinous to him — a crossing can scrape the colour out of a painting he can never repaint.

choices.x: "Tell me only what I can carry alone. I won't spend you on this."
choices.hint: Protect him from the house and the debt by walking into it half-blind. He will let you think you've won the argument, and follow you anyway, one street back, where you can't refuse him.

beats.scene: The name he is not supposed to use
prose: What you are asking, though neither of you says it plainly, is for Itsuki to break a silence he has held for years. He left the Nezu compound the way a man leaves a religion — not loudly, not with a door slammed, but by simply ceasing to answer when the house called his name. The gift that should have made him a Tower never opened in him; it came in sideways, through pigment and a cut palm, and a house that measures its children against a stone older than the lacquer that has gone to glass on it had a word for that, and the word was lesser. To go back now is to put his face in front of that word again, on purpose, for you.

And there is a name he is not supposed to use — a leverage the family pretends does not exist, a debt the house owes his side of it that no Kuroda will speak aloud because speaking it admits it is owed. He turns it over in front of you, this name, the way you turn over a knife you are deciding whether to carry into a room. You watch him decide. He does not perform the cost for you; he just sets his jaw the particular way he sets it before a brushstroke he knows he cannot take back, and reaches for his coat.

Understand what I'm spending, he says, not unkindly, not asking you to stop. The family will move you because I'll make it cheaper for them to move you than to keep refusing me, and they will remember that I made them. They keep accounts longer than anyone alive. By the time the sun's up you'll owe them a number, and I'll owe them the thing under the number. He holds the door. Come on. Your brother's been gone a Wednesday already.

choices.x: "Then don't spend it. We find another road."
choices.hint: Spare him the name and the house — and lose the one route in Tokyo that can read a seated demon for what it is. The other roads are slower, and Gin's lucid windows are closing on a schedule you do not control.

choices.x: "Spend it. I'll find a way to make it right."
choices.hint: Let him pay, and promise a repayment you have no currency for. The Kuroda will hold you to it; so, more quietly, will he — though he will never once name it.

choices.x: Say nothing — just take his coat from the hook and hand it to him.
choices.hint: Answer the way the two of you have always answered each other, beneath words. It settles the matter and it deepens whatever this is between you that neither of you has had the nerve, in fifteen years, to call by its name.

beats.scene: Nezu, the oldest silence in Tokyo
prose: Nezu, where the city keeps its oldest money and its oldest silences. The Kuroda compound does not announce itself — the most private house in Tokyo has never had any need to — only old wood gone black with the decades, a wall that has outlived three governments, and over all of it a stillness that is not peace but attention. The held quiet of a place that has been listening for a very long time and has not yet decided what it thinks of you. The Obon lanterns are out along the lane, small fires for the returning dead, and the compound has hung none; the Kuroda do not invite anything back that they have not first weighed.

A cousin meets you at the gate, and she is not Itsuki's ally. You learn this in the first three seconds, in the flat courtesy she offers him — the courtesy you give a debt that has come to the door on its own legs. She looks at you the way the family looks at everything: past the careful disguise you wear over the two registers you have kept suppressed your whole life, the thing you have never once let anyone see. You feel her find the edge of it and decline, for now, to pull. He brought a stray, she says to Itsuki, not to you. Sei will want to know what kind.

Itsuki does not rise to it, which costs him something you can see and she cannot. He walks the path he was raised on with the particular stiffness of a man in a house that stopped being home the day it measured him and found him short. You walk a half-step behind, watching the rafters, where the wards are old enough to have gone almost decorative, almost — and under the almost, a weight, an attention, the compound deciding by the moment how much of itself to show you.

choices.x: Let your disguise stay shut. Give the house nothing.
choices.hint: Stay a stray, unreadable, safe — and useless to Sei, who trades only in what he can weigh. A house that cannot price you may simply decline to deal.

choices.x: Let the cousin feel one register, on purpose.
choices.hint: Show a hand to buy a hearing. The Kuroda will value you instantly and accurately — and what they learn about you tonight, they keep forever, in the same ledger as Itsuki's debt.

choices.x: Ask the cousin, plainly, why no lanterns.
choices.hint: Press on the one strangeness the house has shown you. The answer is older than Gin's Wednesday, and the family would rather price you than explain it.

beats.scene: Kuroda Sei receives you like deep water receives a stone
prose: Kuroda Sei receives you the way deep water receives a stone — without splash, without resistance, and without any promise that the stone will be given back. He is younger than you expected and stiller than anyone alive, singular among his family for a control that does not look like effort because the effort was finished decades ago. On the low table between you sits the anchor: a teleport-stone the colour of a bruise, the artifact the whole house reaches through, old enough that its lacquer has gone to glass. He does not touch it. He looks at you, and you understand that he has already decided three things about you that you will not be told.

You want a crossing, he says, when he finally speaks, and it is not the crossing he is weighing; it is you. The cost of a crossing is known. The cost of you is not, and my house does not extend credit against an unknown sum. He lets the silence do the asking. The Tower house gives no second chances — not because it is cruel but because it has run the longer numbers and found that mercy, extended twice, becomes a precedent, and a precedent in a house this old becomes a law, and a law it cannot pay it will not write. Itsuki, beside you, has gone very quiet, the quiet of a man whose whole leverage rests on a name nobody will let him say.

And then Sei's attention moves, by a degree, off you and onto the morning you carry — onto the shape of the thing that took your brother — and for the first time something crosses the stillness of his face. Not fear. The family does not fear the way you do. But a recalculation, sudden and total, like a man who has been pricing a coat and abruptly realises he is pricing the man wearing it. What did you say, he asks, very softly, was wrong with the shadow.

choices.x: Describe the wrong shadow exactly — weight where there should be none.
choices.hint: Hand the head of the Tower house the precise shape of what is wearing Gin. He will know it for what it is faster than you want him to, and what the Kuroda know, they act on for their own reasons, not yours.

choices.x: Offer the crossing's price first — name your own debt before he names it.
choices.hint: Take control of the ledger by opening it yourself. Sei respects the move and will charge you no less for it; the house simply prefers a debtor who can count.

choices.x: Ask what made him go still.
choices.hint: Turn his own recalculation back on him. He will tell you only as much as serves the house — and the gap between what he says and what crossed his face is the first true measure you get of how deep the Thirteen runs under all of this.

beats.scene: A wrong shadow carrying weight
prose: The cousin says it before Sei can decide whether to, and the saying of it changes the temperature of the room. A wrong shadow carrying weight. You are describing a seated one. She means the Thirteen, and she does not explain what she means, and the drop in her voice tells you the Kuroda have skin in that game older than your morning, older than the wall outside, older than the grievance they are about to make you pay. For half a heartbeat the most controlled house in Tokyo flinches at a name it does not even speak — and you file that flinch, because a family that fears nothing has just shown you the one thing it does.

Sei recovers first, the way water closes over the stone. He tells you, in the flat cosmological register the family uses for truths that have no pity in them, the part he is willing to spend: that what your brother carries is a Seat of the Thirteen, the register they will only call Duty, and that the Towers — every Tower house, his among them — will not follow it. Not cannot. Will not. There is a line a seated Duty can walk that the oldest powers in the city have agreed, across centuries and without ever writing it down, that they do not walk behind, and the reason is old enough that even Sei gives it to you as a closed door rather than a sentence. If your brother is carrying that seat, he says, then you are not asking me to find a man. You are asking me to look at a thing my house has spent its whole existence learning not to look at.

And there it is — the price, naked at last, and worse than a number. The Kuroda will move you. They will not move toward what is wearing Gin. The house that can fold the city closed in a heartbeat will set you down at the edge of the thing and no nearer, because to step inside the reach of a seated Duty is to risk the one debt even the Tower house cannot file and forget: the debt a seat collects from anyone who acknowledges it. The cousin watches you take this in with something that is almost, not quite, pity. You came in owing us money, she says. You'll leave owing us a silence. Don't tell the lower houses we so much as said the word.

choices.x: Take the edge-crossing. Closer than this you'll walk on your own legs.
choices.hint: Accept the house's limit and the long warded walk past it. You arrive at the threshold of Gin's trail with the family's cosmology in your chest and no one beside you for the last stretch.

choices.x: Push Sei to name what the Towers are afraid of.
choices.hint: Demand the thing behind the closed door. He will not give it whole — but each word you pry loose is a word the house will remember you made it say, and the ledger only ever runs one direction.

choices.x: Promise the silence. Trade what you'll never tell for one thing they will.
choices.hint: Bind yourself to the house's secret in exchange for a true answer. It is a cheap-feeling deal tonight and an iron collar later, when you need the lower houses and cannot prove the one thing that would make them listen.

beats.scene: Back in the studio — he cuts his palm for ink
prose: The family will set you at the edge, but the edge is not the same as a sight, and the one sight in Tokyo you would trust on your own brother belongs to the man scraping bruise-coloured residue off his fingers beside you. Back in the studio, the sky going grey at the high windows, Itsuki turns the worst canvas to face the room — the Ōji overpass at dusk, the one he could never finish — and you finally see the shape he has been almost-painting and scraping out for weeks. A figure on the bridge, its shadow thrown forward, into the light it should have been falling away from. He has been painting Gin's wrongness for a month without knowing whose it was.

I can make it a door, he says, the way he said it in another life, on another road, except this time he says it knowing the house's word for what is on the far side. I can't make it a safe one. And I've never carried a person and a question at the same time. He means he can turn his sight on Gin through the painting — read the seam you have been straining to hear on the phone, the place where your brother ends and the seated thing begins — but to look at a Duty that close is to let it look back, and to spend, in the looking, colour he is not certain will come back to his hands. The whole of his gift is borrowed against paintings he has not made yet. This would be a withdrawal he cannot see the balance behind.

He picks up the blade he keeps for this, the little one with the worn handle, and holds it over his palm, and waits — not for your permission exactly, but for you to be the one who decides what you are about to ask of him. The cut is the easy part. The cut is just ink. What he is offering you is the harder thing, and he is making you hold it in your own hand before he opens his.

choices.x: "Look. I need to know where my brother ends."
choices.hint: Ask him to spend it. You will get the seam — the exact border between Gin and the Healer wearing him — and Itsuki will get whatever the looking costs, which neither of you can price until it's already gone.

choices.x: "Don't. I've taken enough from you tonight."
choices.hint: Refuse the gift to spare the giver, and carry into Book Two only the family's cold cosmology, without the one intimate, human reading of your brother that might have told you he is still in there.

choices.x: "Look — but you pull out the second it bites back."
choices.hint: Try to bound the cost in advance. He will agree, and you both know that a man reading a seated Duty does not get to choose the moment he stops; the seat chooses.

beats.scene: The shadow thrown forward
prose: He cuts, and dips, and lays the wet red line along the figure on the bridge, and the studio goes the particular silent of a held breath, and then the painting opens — not a door you step through this time but a window his sight throws onto your brother, wherever Gin is, north, toward water. And you see them at last, the two of them, layered in the one body the way Itsuki layers a canvas: underneath, faint and frightened and unmistakably Gin, the brother who told you on the phone to go home; over him, even and reasonable and patient, the seated thing the family will only call Duty, the one Yushiro names to himself, when he bothers with names, the Healer. The seam between them is not a wall. It is a tide. It comes in over your brother and goes out and comes in again, and in the going-out you can see exactly how much of Gin is left, and it is enough to save and not enough to wait.

This is the gift the road gives you, and it feeds straight into the Handwriting: you no longer have to learn the seam by ear, one stolen lucid sentence at a time. You have seen it whole. You know the shape of the thing's argument now — that the dead of the north were never given their due, that the membrane over Kita-ku is a wound a high enough grief could finally close, that catastrophe seen from a vacant Thirteenth Seat looks like an obligation met at last — and you know, because Itsuki's sight showed you the frightened register underneath, that your brother does not believe it and cannot stop his own mouth from saying it. The Healer is not lying to Gin. It is reasoning with him, in his own cadence, and winning by inches.

Then it bites back. The figure on the bridge turns its thrown-forward shadow toward the window, the way a man turns toward a draught he didn't know was open, and Itsuki makes a sound you have never heard him make. You break the contact the only way you can, with your whole body, and when it's done he is sitting on the studio floor and the canvas on the easel is blank — scraped clean by nothing you did, the overpass gone, the figure gone, the month of work gone — and when he reaches for it his fingers find the surface and no colour will come.

choices.x: Go to him first. The trail can hold for a breath.
choices.hint: Choose the friend over the lead. Gin is still north and still going; the seconds you spend on the studio floor are seconds the tide takes back — but Itsuki, white and shaking and unable to find his own colour, is the cost of this road made flesh, and he is in front of you now.

choices.x: Fix the heading first, while the sight is fresh.
choices.hint: Pin down exactly where the window showed Gin before the image fades. You'll lose nothing of the trail and a little of yourself — Itsuki will tell you he's fine, and you will choose, this once, to be told.

choices.x: Ask him what he saw that you couldn't.
choices.hint: His sight is older than yours and reads layers you only felt. He saw something in the tide he hasn't said — and prying it out of a man who just lost his colour for you is a thing you will have to decide whether you are.

beats.scene: What you owe, and to whom
prose: You come back to the morning owing a debt with no number on it, and Itsuki owing the house more, and the city sitting a half-degree off true from the places you have stood tonight where no one should stand. The Kuroda have what they wanted, which was your measure; you have what you came for, which is worse and better than a location — you have the seam, the tide, the proof that your brother is still in there and the timing that says not for long. The Towers will not follow a seated Duty. You will. That gap, between what the oldest house in Tokyo has decided it cannot afford and what you cannot afford not to do, is the whole shape of the road you have just walked, and it points north, toward water, the way every road on this morning eventually does.

Itsuki gets up off the floor, because he is the kind of man who gets up, and he turns the blank canvas back to the wall the way you turn a photograph of someone you are not ready to have died. It'll come back, he says, of the colour, and you both let it be true in the room even though neither of you knows it. He does not ask you what you'll do with what he spent to show you. He has known you fifteen years; he already knows you'll spend it, all of it, the way you spend everything, on Gin. The not-asking is the most he will let himself say, and you hear all of it.

What you carry out of the studio into Book Two is the family's cold cosmology and one warm, ruinous reading laid over it: that the thing wearing your brother has a seat to claim and a wall to thin and a perfectly reasonable case, and that the man under it is awake enough to be afraid and not free enough to run. The lanterns are guttering along the Nezu lane as you leave — the small fires the Kuroda lit for nothing, hung for no returning dead — and you understand, with the half-degree of new wrongness the night has put in you, exactly why a house that old declines to invite anything back across a membrane it has spent its whole existence learning not to thin.

choices.x: North, now, on the heading the sight gave you.
choices.hint: Carry the road straight into the Handwriting and go after Gin while the tide still leaves enough of him to reach. You go with the seam in your eyes and a friend behind you who cannot paint.

choices.x: Make the repayment to Itsuki first, whatever it costs you.
choices.hint: Refuse to leave the studio owing the one debt that was never the house's. There is no currency for it and you go looking anyway — which is either the most honest thing you do all night or the slowest.

choices.x: Keep the Kuroda's silence — and start counting what it will cost you later.
choices.hint: Honour the trade you made with the cousin and feel the collar of it settle. The lower houses, the Grid, the CVD: every road after this one is harder for the word you have promised never to say.

cvd.title: The Directorate
acts: Open: become theirs to be allowed in
Deepen: the briefing Gin skipped, from the inside
Converge: the file that should not exist

beats.scene: CVD intake, Kasumigaseki, before the desks fill
prose: The Civil Veil Directorate does not look like a place that crosses to the dead. It looks like every other ministry annex in Kasumigaseki at this hour — fluorescent strip light over grey carpet tile, a vending machine humming to no one, a wall clock that has been forty seconds slow for so long that the staff have stopped trusting it. You came here because every other door you tried this morning gave you a brother-shaped silence, and the one institution that should have logged Gin missing has logged nothing at all. That nothing is the loudest thing in Tokyo right now, and the only way to read it is from inside.

Registration is not a form. It is a small white room and a woman named Okada Shizuka who does not ask your name because she has known it, you slowly realize, for four years. She slides a single laminated card across the table — the Postulate, they call it, the test that decides whether the city files you as a citizen who saw something or a medium who is something — and she watches your hands more than your face while you read it. Most people lie on this without meaning to, she says, not unkindly. The veil doesn't care what you wish were true. Neither do we. Behind her, Obon decorations someone hung without conviction sag in the air-conditioning: paper lanterns for the returning dead, in the one building in the country that knows exactly how literally to take them.

You understand, holding the card, that this is the first door and that it only opens one way. To present cleanly — to let them read you, name you, file you — is to hand the Directorate a key to the part of yourself you have spent your whole life keeping two locks ahead of everyone. But the alternative is to stay outside, where Gin's absence is a private grief instead of an institutional fact, and grief has never once told you where someone went.

choices.x: Present clean. Let the Postulate read you true.
choices.hint: They will know exactly what you are by lunchtime — both registers, the searching, all of it. A medium files faster than a citizen. So does a liability.

choices.x: Present as a witness, not a medium. Hold one register back.
choices.hint: Slower clearance, smaller access — but they file you as ordinary, and the part of you that frightens you stays yours. Gin's trail is behind doors a witness never reaches.

choices.x: Ask Okada why she already knows your name.
choices.hint: She will tell you, and what she tells you will mean your brother prepared this room for you years ago — which means he knew, years ago, that you would one day need it.

beats.scene: Director Adachi's office, two floors above the carpet tile
prose: Director Adachi keeps his office colder than the rest of the building and his voice warmer, and you spend the first minute trying to decide which one is the lie. He has your file open — thin, suspiciously thin for a man who registered an hour ago — and he reads from it the way a doctor reads a chart he has already memorized, for your benefit, to let you feel consulted. Uedera's brother, he says, and lets the surname sit in the cold air between you. He spoke of you. Not often. Once, properly. He does not say when. You will spend weeks deciding the when mattered.

What Adachi offers is real and the catch is also real, and he is too good at this to pretend otherwise. Clearance, casework, the ladder — the Directorate will let you climb toward the floors where your brother's name still lives in active systems, but every rung is a thing the institution does to you in exchange. You will carry their flag to scenes. You will file what you find in the shape they prefer it filed. And somewhere above this office, in rooms Adachi gestures at without looking, are the five families who decide which of the Directorate's truths survive contact with their interests. I am the ceiling you can see, he tells you, almost gently. I'd rather you knew that now than discovered it at a worse hour.

Okada is in the room and says nothing, which you are learning is how she says the most. When Adachi steps out to take a call he was always going to take, she leans in and gives you the only thing she has been waiting four years to give: that Gin's last instruction to her, the one he left like a stone in a riverbed for the current to uncover, was not protect the Directorate and not find me. It was when my brother comes, do not let them assess him on a Thursday. She does not know why. You are starting to.

choices.x: Take the ladder. Climb toward Gin's name, on their terms.
choices.hint: Access opens fast. So does the slow conversion of you into the institution's instrument — by the time you reach his floor you may be the kind of person who would file him away.

choices.x: Take only enough clearance to work cases, refuse the climb.
choices.hint: Stay small enough that the families never notice you. You also stay small enough that the doors with your brother behind them stay shut a great deal longer.

choices.x: Ask Okada what happens on Thursdays.
choices.hint: She will tell you it is assessment day, when the Auditors read mediums down to the registers — and that something about you, read on a Thursday, is what Gin spent his last free act trying to prevent.

beats.scene: First clearance, first call-out, Kita-ku after dark
prose: Your first scene is a fourth-floor walk-up in Kita where a woman has been hearing her late husband run the bath at 3:47 every morning, and you are not the lead. The lead is Nakamura Aoi, junior like you but a year deeper, and she works a haunting the way other people defuse something — slowly, with her whole attention, narrating nothing she does not have to. She clocks your registers the instant the cold front of the apartment touches you, you can see her clock it, and the only thing she says is breathe out before you reach, not in, which is the first useful thing anyone in this building has ever told you about what you are.

Kato Ryusei takes the report, because Kato takes every report, and his eyes do the small soft thing they do when Aoi speaks that he has not yet noticed they do. The case itself is ordinary in the worst way — a man who died with one unfinished motion and a wife who cannot stop hearing him try to complete it — and you watch Aoi cross just far enough to tell him the bath is run, it has been run, he can stop, and then come back with her hands shaking and her face perfectly still. That's the job, she says afterward on the stairwell, not looking at you. You go where they're stuck and you tell them it's done. The trick is believing it on the way back.

It is on those stairs, with the lantern-smell of Obon coming up the well from someone's open window, that Aoi mentions Gin without knowing she is handing you a knife. She worked one rotation under him. She noticed when he stopped coming in. And the thing that has bothered her since — the thing she has not filed because there is no field on the form for it — is that the absence is the wrong shape. A man who quits leaves a quitting-shaped hole. Gin left something else. She does not have the word. You do, and you do not say it, because to say it on a stairwell at Obon to a near-stranger is to make it true.

choices.x: Tell Aoi the word. Trust her with the shape.
choices.hint: She is the first person in the building who saw it too. Trust bought this early is real — and it makes her a person the institution can now hurt to get to you.

choices.x: Say nothing. Let her keep the question.
choices.hint: Protect her by leaving her with a mystery instead of a target. You also walk the rest of this road one ally lighter, carrying the shape alone.

choices.x: Ask her what Gin was working when the shape changed.
choices.hint: She will give you a date and a district — Kita, the low places near the water — and a date is a thread, and threads in this building are how the families find out you are pulling.

beats.scene: The briefing archive, the Thursday that has a hole in it
prose: Every briefing the Directorate runs is logged, transcribed, and shelved, which means somewhere in this building is the record of the last briefing your brother attended and the record of the first one in nine years that he did not. You requisition them both. The clearance you spent to do it costs you a favour you will not understand the price of until later, but the woman at the records cage stamps the slip without reading it, because at this hour even the Directorate runs on people too tired to ask why.

The attended briefings read like a man at the top of his craft — Gin's questions in the margins, sharp, three moves ahead of the room, the handwriting you would know in the dark. And then the Thursday. The transcript exists; the seat does not. There is a gap in the round-table log shaped exactly like a Vanguard who was expected and did not come, and the remarkable thing, the thing that lifts the hair on your arms in the over-lit cage, is that no one chased it. A man who has not missed a Thursday in nine years skips one and the system simply closes around the space — a sign-off here, a reassignment there, a note in a hand you do not recognize saying the matter was handled at a level above the room. Handled, in this building, you are learning, is a verb that means buried with permission.

You read the after-action on the case that briefing was meant to cover, and it is the wrong kind of clean. A drowning in the Kita lowlands, the low place where the water remembers, closed in under two days with a confidence the evidence does not earn. Whoever signed it wanted it gone. And tucked in the appendix, a body-reading you were not cleared to see, initialled by a specialist named Kurosawa — three lines, then redaction, then the only words that survived the black bar: double-layer. not consistent with the registered subject. recommend escalation. The escalation never happened. Someone above the room decided your brother's body was a sentence best left unfinished.

choices.x: Find Kurosawa. Ask what 'double-layer' means.
choices.hint: He read your brother and lived to redact it. He can tell you what is wearing Gin — but a specialist who talks twice is a specialist Internal Affairs starts watching, and so are his visitors.

choices.x: Pull the thread on who signed the Thursday away.
choices.hint: The signature leads up, toward the families and the floors Adachi only gestured at. Follow it and you stop being a junior reading files and start being a problem with a name.

choices.x: Copy the redacted reading and tell no one yet.
choices.hint: Evidence in your pocket is leverage and liability in one envelope. The Directorate has rooms for people who walk out with what they were not cleared to keep.

beats.scene: Kurosawa's lab, where the bodies are read and not believed
prose: Kurosawa works in a sub-level the building pretends is storage, and he reads bodies the way a restorer reads a painting that has been painted over — looking for the under-image, the thing the surface was put there to hide. He is not surprised you found him. He has been waiting, in the specific way of a man who did the right thing once, filed it, watched it vanish, and has been living since inside the question of whether he should have shouted instead. When you say the word double-layer he stops pretending to work.

What he tells you, carefully, with the door watched, is the physiology of a haunting that is not a haunting. Possession in the Directorate's textbooks is a fever — a thing that rides hot and clumsy and burns its host out in weeks. What he read in Gin was the opposite: cold, patient, tidy, a second register laid down under the first as deliberately as a second coat of paint, a presence that was not consuming the host but preserving him, keeping him functional, keeping him filing, keeping him at his desk nine days a week. I have read a great many possessed, Kurosawa says. I have never read one being taken care of. Whatever is in your brother does not want him dead. It wants him working.

He gives you the name of the only operational fact that survived the cover-up — a clerk named Tanaka, who sits behind Kurosawa in the org chart and in front of him in the chain that buried the reading, and who knows the single concrete thing the redaction was built to hide: not what Gin is, but where the recommendation went when escalation was denied. A name on a routing slip. A floor. I read the symptom, Kurosawa says, already turning back to his work, already rehearsing his innocence. Tanaka can tell you who decided the symptom was convenient. After that you are on your own, and so, I'm afraid, is your brother.

choices.x: Go to Tanaka straight, before the building closes around it.
choices.hint: Speed beats the cover-up, but a junior who sprints from Kurosawa's lab to a routing clerk draws a line on a map that Internal Affairs can read as easily as you can.

choices.x: Bring it to Moriya in Internal Affairs first.
choices.hint: IA is the one body that can subpoena up past Adachi — or the one body that can make a discrepancy, and the person carrying it, both quietly disappear. You will not know which Moriya is until you are inside the room.

choices.x: Sit with what Kurosawa said: it wants Gin working. Ask why.
choices.hint: The answer reframes everything — a demon that preserves its host is a demon with a project — but following the thought means admitting your brother is not a victim being drained, he is a tool being maintained, and toward what you do not yet dare to guess.

beats.scene: Katagiri Noa, and the months that were never filed
prose: Noa agrees to meet you because you are his brother and refuses to meet you anywhere with a Directorate camera, which tells you most of what the conversation will be before it starts. She loved Gin — two years adjacent, the kind of love that is mostly proximity and unspoken timing and one missed window — and she carried something of his for the last months that she never put in a single report, because the form would have made it evidence and she did not want him to be evidence yet. Across a café table in Nippori, with the Obon crowds thick outside and the lanterns going up along the shōtengai, she finally makes him evidence, for you.

He changed, she says, not all at once. The work got better and the man got worse — sharper case-closure rates and a new, terrible patience, as if someone had taken her colleague and ironed him flat. He started talking about duty the way the devout talk about grace, an interrupted duty, a thing left undischarged, and once, late, after a closing they should have celebrated, he had looked at the Kita lowlands across the water and said a sentence she has not been able to set down since: The wall is thinner there than the maps admit, and somebody has to decide whether thin is the same as wrong. She thought it was exhaustion. She is telling you now because she has finally understood it was a plan, said out loud, by something using his mouth and his exhaustion as cover.

Then she gives you the thing she has been protecting, the unfiled truth that is also the kindest and cruelest fact you will carry out of this road: that in his last lucid month, Gin came to her once, briefly, all the way himself — she could tell, she will always be able to tell — and asked her to make sure that if anyone ever came looking, they understood he had not chosen this and could not, now, choose out of it alone. He didn't ask me to save him, Noa says, and does not cry, which is worse. He asked me to make sure someone knew the difference between him and the thing wearing him. I think he meant you.

choices.x: Promise Noa you'll hold the difference, whatever it costs.
choices.hint: It is the right promise and the one you cannot fully keep — the deeper you go, the harder it gets to tell the brother from the thing, and a promise like this can become the rope you hang on.

choices.x: Ask for everything she remembers about the Kita lowlands.
choices.hint: She has been to the low place with him. What she remembers is a map no file holds — and walking it means walking toward the exact wall your brother's borrower wants thinned.

choices.x: Ask whether she'd testify, if it came to Internal Affairs.
choices.hint: Her word could break the cover-up open. It would also put the woman who loved your brother in front of the families' machinery, and she has already lost him once.

beats.scene: Public Confidence, where files are kept clean by being emptied
prose: Hagiwara Mizuki runs the office the Directorate does not advertise, the one called Public Confidence, whose job is not to lie to the city but to decide which truths the city can survive knowing — and she summons you, which means you have become a truth she is now weighing. Her office is the warmest room in the building and the most dangerous, full of soft light and good tea and the unhurried manner of a person who has erased better-credentialed people than you before the second cup. She knows about the requisition. The Kurosawa copy. The visit to Noa. She lays your last week out on the table like a hand of cards she has already won, and then she does the thing that nearly works: she is reasonable.

There is an address, she explains, that does not exist. A case closed too fast, a body-reading that recommends an escalation the institution chose not to survive, a Vanguard whose absence was handled above the room — and all of it, she says, is true, and all of it, she says, is also a wall holding back a flood you cannot see the size of. The five families did not bury your brother out of cruelty, she tells you, refilling your cup. They buried him because the alternative was a panic this city is not built to hold. You can have the truth or you can have the city standing the morning after. I have spent my career learning you almost never get both. She offers you the address. She offers you a future in the Directorate. The price is that you take the second in exchange for never speaking the first.

And here is the trap, the elegant centre of it: she is not entirely wrong. Some part of what she says is the most honest thing anyone in this building has told you. The membrane in the Kita lowlands is thinning, the panic would be real, and a younger, frightened version of you would take the deal and call it maturity. But you have read the under-image now. You know the thing wearing your brother is not a flood the families are containing — it is a project they have decided is cheaper to permit than to fight, and Mizuki's reasonable, grieving city is the alibi a thinned wall hides behind. The clean file she is offering you is not a kindness. It is the last door, and it only opens one way.

choices.x: Take the address. Trade your silence for the door.
choices.hint: You reach the place no file admits — and you arrive as the institution's instrument, having already practiced, once, the act of filing a truth away. The first time is the hardest. She is counting on there being a second.

choices.x: Refuse, and walk out carrying everything you've found.
choices.hint: You keep your mouth and lose the door, the ladder, and the protection. The families do not forgive a junior who chooses the flood over the wall, and you have just told the warmest room in the building exactly what you are.

choices.x: Pretend to take the deal. Let her think the wall held.
choices.hint: Buy the address with a lie and walk out still yourself — but Mizuki erases better liars than you for a living, and a deal you intend to break is a debt that comes due at the worst possible hour.

beats.scene: The file that should not exist, read at last by its own light
prose: However you came by it — bought, stolen, or refused into your hands by accident — the address that no file admits is real, and it is in the Kita lowlands, the low place where the water remembers, the wall your brother said was thinner than the maps allow. You stand in the records cage one last time with the institution's own paper in your hands and you understand, finally, what the Directorate was for in this road: not to hide your brother from you, but to teach you to read the way he learned to read, in the demanded order, one buried node at a time, until the shape underneath the shape stands up off the page and looks back.

Because it is all here, in the cleanest filing in Tokyo. The skipped briefing was not Gin avoiding his duty; it was the borrower keeping the host away from a room where a sharp colleague might have read the cold under his skin. The case closed too fast was the lowland drowning — a soul that crossed too easily, through a wall already going thin, evidence the project was working. The body-reading buried above the room was the truth filed where the truth goes to be convenient. And the five families' reasonable, grieving silence is the permission a Duty-register demon needed to keep your brother at his desk, productive, preserved, plotting the thinning of the Kita membrane behind nine years of perfect attendance and a single, deliberate, telling absence.

You leave the Directorate the way you came, through the lobby and the sagging Obon lanterns and the wall clock that is still forty seconds slow, and nothing about you looks different to the tired people at the desks. But you are carrying the institution's own hand back to the Handwriting now — the dates, the routing slip, the word double-layer, the name Yushiro you have not yet let yourself say aloud — and for the first time since the cold kitchen and the 3:47 that started all of this, you are not chasing a brother-shaped silence. You are reading the thing that made the silence, in its own ledger, in the order it demanded, toward the wall it wants thinned. The Directorate gave you the only honest gift it had: it taught you to see the project. What you do with the seeing belongs to the books that come after.

choices.x: Take the file to the Kita lowlands. Read the wall yourself.
choices.hint: The next truth is at the thinning place, not in any cage. But the borrower wanted you reading paper, not standing at the membrane — arrive there and you arrive where the project can see you back.

choices.x: Carry it back to the Handwriting. Cross-read it against Gin's own nodes.
choices.hint: His Archive and the Directorate's file are the same map drawn by enemy hands. Laid together they name Yushiro — and naming it is the moment the searching ends and the harder thing begins.

choices.x: Burn your copy. Keep only what you can carry in your head.
choices.hint: Paper can be subpoenaed, planted, or used to bury you the way it buried the reading. Memory can't be requisitioned — but memory is also the one record the thing wearing your brother already knows how to edit.
